articles.fullText:
China's manufacturing competitiveness is increasingly being shaped by technological innovation and industrial upgrading. China now hosts 109 of the world's 238 lighthouse factories, or 45.8% of the global total, ranking first in the world, according to the World Economic Forum's latest Lighthouse Network figures.
A recently released Ministry of Commerce document emphasizes that the rapid growth of China's modern industries is being driven by innovation. The numbers tell the story: by June 2026, 89.6% of industrial enterprises above designated size had undergone digital transformation and the country had cumulatively cultivated over 8,000 national-level green factories and more than 600 green industrial parks. Together, they point to an undeniable truth – the competitiveness of China's manufacturing capacity stems from technological innovation and industrial upgrading.
Among China's 109 lighthouses, the industries span automobiles, home appliances, electronics, new energy and more. At the Haier Shenyang Refrigerator Interconnected Factory, the world's first end-to-end lighthouse in the refrigerator industry, a single production line supports flexible mass customization of over 500 models, with a production "Takt Time" shortened to one unit every 10 seconds. Through an expandable digital platform, the factory has achieved end-to-end connectivity across the entire value chain, raising direct labor productivity by 28%.
A lighthouse factory in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, May 16, 2026. 
"The lighthouse factory represents a stepping stone toward an even more advanced model – a 'factory brain'," said Yuan Haidong, general manager of the intelligent manufacturing department at Hisense Visual Technology. At the Hisense Qingdao factory – the only lighthouse in the global television manufacturing industry – the adoption of AI, big data, simulation and large-scale virtual reality throughout R&D and manufacturing reduced Research and Development cycles by 34%, lowered material costs by 18%, and cut new employee training time by 60%.
Beyond individual factories, China's digital transformation is reshaping the geography of manufacturing itself.
In the Yangtze River Delta, Shanghai focuses on chips and high-end wafer research and development, Jiangsu leads in semiconductor packaging and testing, Anhui pursues storage and display driver wafer foundry via companies such as ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and Nexchip Semiconductor Corporation, and Zhejiang specializes in design and semiconductor supporting materials.
This differentiated division of labor has created a functional innovation system where leading enterprises or research institutes propose technical needs and recruit regional universities, research institutes and supply chain partners to jointly tackle core technologies – breaking the traditional linear path of "basic research-results-industrialization" in favor of direct, point-to-point industrial innovation.
A low-carbon wastewater treatment plant in Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, June 16, 2026. 
Green capacity – lowering the cost of the global energy transition
China stays focused on empowerment through innovation, contributing to significantly greener and smarter traditional industries. China supports enterprises in adopting digital and smart technologies to drive industrial optimization and upgrading and promoting higher-end, smarter and greener industries.
According to the Ministry of Commerce document, in recent years, industries in China have grown increasingly eco-friendly. Over 8,000 national green factories and more than 600 green industrial parks have been built, and the 246 national green data centers are 50% powered by green electricity. Of all industrial enterprises above the designated size, 89.6% have launched digital transformation and 57.7% have installed digital equipment. China has 109 lighthouse factories, nearly half of the global total.
According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), since 2010, the cost of photovoltaic power generation has fallen by 89%, concentrated solar power by 72%, onshore wind by 71% and offshore wind by 63%. IRENA explicitly notes that the intense competition in the global renewable energy industry – driven in large part by the massive expansion of Chinese manufacturing – has compressed profit margins to extremely low levels, with prices approaching production costs.

articles.titleCn: 远程医疗改变科特迪瓦医疗服务的获取方式
articles.summary: In Côte d'Ivoire, seeing a doctor no longer necessarily means spending hours travelling to a hospital or waiting for a consultation.
articles.summaryCn: 科特迪瓦的Umed电子健康中心通过远程医疗和上门服务，为阿比让居民提供了便捷的医疗选择，减轻了医院压力。

paragraphs.en: In Côte d'Ivoire, seeing a doctor no longer necessarily means spending hours travelling to a hospital or waiting for a {{2}}. Since 2019, the Umed eHealth Center has used telemedicine to connect doctors with patients across Abidjan, offering an {{15}} to conventional consultations in a city where traffic {{1}} and long distances can make accessing healthcare challenging. From behind a computer screen, Dr. Esther Kassi-Aleba begins a consultation with a patient several kilometers away. The patient is unable to travel to a healthcare facility, but through a video call, Kassi-Aleba can listen to her concerns, ask questions and {{3}} her {{4}} remotely.
paragraphs.cn: 在科特迪瓦，看医生不再意味着花几个小时去医院或等待咨询。自2019年以来，Umed电子健康中心利用远程医疗将医生与阿比让各地的患者连接起来，在交通拥堵和距离遥远可能使就医变得困难的城市中，提供了一种传统咨询的替代方案。在电脑屏幕后面，埃斯特·卡西-阿莱巴医生开始与几公里外的患者进行咨询。患者无法前往医疗机构，但通过视频通话，卡西-阿莱巴可以倾听她的担忧、提问并远程评估她的症状。

paragraphs.en:

There are no crowded waiting rooms or lengthy journeys — just an internet connection connecting the patient to medical care. "We realized that for simple tests, such as a malaria test or minor symptoms, patients can face very long waiting times in hospitals," says Kassi-Aleba, a doctor at the Umed eHealth Center. "We decided to take some of the {{5}} off hospitals by managing these minor conditions while using technology to improve access to healthcare."
From the screen to the patient's home
But the consultation does not always end online. When a patient requires a physical examination or treatment, the center can {{6}} a medical team to their home.

With our family, and with a little family love, this enables us to recover better — or let's say, to recover more quickly," she says. Since 2019, the Umed eHealth Center has used telemedicine to connect doctors with patients across Abidjan, offering an alternative to conventional consultations in a city where traffic congestion and long distances can make accessing healthcare challenging.
From behind a computer screen, Dr. Esther Kassi-Aleba begins a consultation with a patient several kilometers away.
The patient is unable to travel to a healthcare facility, but through a video call, Kassi-Aleba can listen to her concerns, ask questions and assess her symptoms remotely.
A patient being checked in her house in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, August 23, 2026. 
 Africa
There are no crowded waiting rooms or lengthy journeys — just an internet connection connecting the patient to medical care.
"We realized that for simple tests, such as a malaria test or minor symptoms, patients can face very long waiting times in hospitals," says Kassi-Aleba, a doctor at the Umed eHealth Center. "We decided to take some of the pressure off hospitals by managing these minor conditions while using technology to improve access to healthcare."
From the screen to the patient's home
But the consultation does not always end online.
When a patient requires a physical examination or treatment, the center can dispatch a medical team to their home.
Kassi-Aleba says receiving care in familiar surroundings can also make the recovery process more comfortable.
"We recover more quickly at home. With our family, and with a little family love, this enables us to recover better — or let's say, to recover more quickly," she says.
On one such visit, Nurse Micheline Apete prepares to make a home call.
"We're going to Attoban to see a patient suffering from abdominal pain. She has a fever, headaches and vomiting. Following the doctor's instructions, we're going to treat her," Apete says.
Minutes later, the medical team arrives at the patient's home and begins treatment based on the doctor's instructions.
The patient receives intravenous paracetamol to help reduce her fever, along with other prescribed medication.
"We gave her intravenous paracetamol to bring down her fever. The doctor prescribed a treatment plan, including a vitamin complex to give her a boost. She'll feel better in about 10 minutes," Apete says.
For Seynabou Messou, telemedicine has been part of her healthcare routine for seven years, August 23, 2026. 
 Africa
Care without leaving home
For Seynabou Messou, who has used the service for seven years, telemedicine has become part of her healthcare routine.
After years of navigating Abidjan's traffic and hospital queues, she says receiving medical care at home has made a significant difference.
"I'm not too keen on hospital beds, so I prefer to be 'hospitalized' at home, in my bedroom or living room. What's changed for me is that there's always a team on hand, whatever the time, and I don't need to travel to access care — even for blood tests and test results," Messou says.
The Umed eHealth Center says it receives about five requests for remote consultations each day.
Remote consultations and home visits are included in its treatment packages, providing an alternative for patients seeking more convenient access to healthcare.
A nurse browsing the telemedicine app on her machine in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, August 23, 2026. 
 Africa
Telemedicine has its limits
Technology, however, cannot replace every aspect of medical care.
The center mainly manages minor conditions remotely. Patients who require surgery, resuscitation or other specialized treatment are referred to appropriate medical facilities.
For now, the combination of telemedicine and home-based care is offering some residents of Abidjan a simpler way to access medical attention — without having to leave home.
As technology continues to reshape healthcare delivery, Côte d'Ivoire's experience shows how digital tools can help bring doctors closer to patients while easing some of the pressure on conventional health facilities.

(ECNS) -- With the Mid-Autumn Festival still more than three weeks away, mooncakes made especially for cats and dogs are already on sale in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, with some sellers expecting demand to rise by about 30 percent from last year, the Chengdu Commercial Daily reported Thursday.
Pet food shops began taking pre-orders in mid-August, weeks earlier than in previous years, as owners look to celebrate the holiday with their pets by buying treats shaped like paws, lions and rabbits.
Zhou Xitong, who runs the Beian Sisters Fresh Pet Food store, said she has already sold more than 300 gift boxes and expects to sell more than 600 — around 2,400 mooncakes — before the festival. A box of four sells for 68 yuan (about $9.60).
Unlike traditional mooncakes filled with lotus seed paste or salted egg yolk, the pet versions contain ingredients including chicken, duck, beef liver, rabbit, chicken heart, beef and salmon, along with pumpkin, sweet potato, yam and goat's milk powder.
Zhou said her shop began taking pre-orders early to give staff enough time to keep up with demand.
"In previous years, many pet owners only remembered at the last minute that they wanted to buy a mooncake for their cat or dog," she said. "From our experience, pre-orders and last-minute orders each account for about half of sales. Later on, it's not that there are no customers — it's that we don't have enough hands and simply can't make them fast enough."
Kang Xinyue, who handles online sales for GoFine, another fresh pet food maker, said the company opened pre-orders on Sept. 1 this year, compared with just a week before the festival last year. More than 10 orders came in on the morning the announcement was posted, she said.
GoFine received nearly 100 orders last year and expects sales to grow by about 30 percent this year, Kang said.
Pet boarding services are also filling up ahead of the holiday, which this year falls close to the weeklong National Day holiday in early October.
An employee surnamed Zhou at Xingyunshu (Lucky Tree) Pet said the shop has already received five or six boarding reservations for the Mid-Autumn Festival, with about half of its kennel spaces booked. In previous years, he said, spaces are typically fully booked around 10 days before a holiday.
Behind the growing demand for festive treats is a broader shift in how Chinese people view and care for their pets.
Cao Juan, manager of a pet store in Chengdu's Jinniu district, said her customers range from people in their 20s to families in their 30s and 40s, as well as elderly residents. Younger owners, in particular, tend to treat their pets like children, she said.
"They treat their pets like children," Cao said. "Whatever children have, they want their pets to have, too."
The shop also sells fresh pet food and birthday cakes, including custom cakes decorated with a pet's face based on a photograph. Cao said an elaborate portrait cake can take several hours to make and may cost more than a cake for people, but customers are still willing to pay for it.
Zhou said more pet owners in Chengdu are making fresh food a regular part of their animals' diets. Some order treats or "afternoon tea" for their pets on weekends and have them delivered the same day.
Kang said people in their 60s are also a core group of customers. Many are retirees whose children live elsewhere, with pets providing them with companionship, she said.
"They also transfer the love they have for their children onto their pets," Kang said.
The mooncakes have also become increasingly popular as gifts. Kang said buyers are increasingly bringing boxes when visiting friends or relatives who own dogs. The company also received corporate orders for pet zongzi during this year's Dragon Boat Festival, with employers buying them as benefits for staff members who own pets.

China's open AI models have surpassed 10 billion cumulative downloads worldwide. But the real story lies not in the sheer volume – it lies in what the global open community actually builds with them.
According to Hugging Face's Summer 2026 report published on August 14, Chinese-developed open models now dominate the frontier of AI scale. In almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released – with China's monthly ceiling ranging between 754 billion and 2.78 trillion parameters, while US models stayed under 130 billion in five of seven months.
/Hugging Face
More tellingly, Chinese models are not just downloaded – they are built upon. Derivatives based on Alibaba's Qwen alone now number 151,448 on the Hugging Face Hub, 2.6 times Meta's total footprint. That figure grows by 180 to 210 new repositories every single day.
These are not just statistics – they represent a fundamental shift in how advanced technology reaches the world. Unlike proprietary models that charge hefty licensing fees, China's open models are freely downloadable, commercially usable and highly adaptable.
This open approach allows more countries, especially developing countries, to access and afford cutting-edge AI technology, said Yan Dong, vice minister of commerce.
From Silicon Valley startups to European manufacturing plants, overseas companies are actively adopting Chinese open models – such as DeepSeek and Qwen – as their technology backbone. A partner at Andreessen Horowitz revealed that as many as 80% of AI startups seeking funding in Silicon Valley use Chinese open models. One model, adapted with local African data, now supports 20 African languages.
China's commitment to openness extends far beyond software. In March, the Zhongguancun Forum released the Open Science International Cooperation Action Plan, opening 10 major research infrastructure facilities to global scientists.
These include the EAST "artificial sun" fusion reactor – which has cooperated with over 120 research institutions across more than 50 countries, according to reports from China Media Group – and the "Tianyan‑P2000" photonic quantum computer, the first photonic quantum computer with quantum supremacy capability open to global users.
Citizens visit the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST) nuclear fusion device, Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, May 17, 2025. 
The Synergetic Extreme Condition User Facility, completed in 2025, has already served 381 institutions, including 16 international organizations from 11 countries, with open beam time reaching 428,000 hours.
A technician works at the Synergetic Extreme Condition User Facility in Huairou Science City, Beijing, China, July 16, 2026. 
If China's technological capacity was truly a "threat," why would it open up its most advanced AI models and grant global access to its most sophisticated research facilities? The answer is clear: China's tech capacity is not a closed proprietary asset but an open global public good – one that empowers rather than threatens, and invites the world to share the benefits of scientific progress.
